proofs.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\) and a cohort \(d\in\{0,1\}\).  All probabilities in the first part of the proof are conditional on \(D=d\), which is legitimate by \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\).  For \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), define the proof intermediates
\[
 B_x[u,j]=P(X_0=u,X_1=x,Z=j\mid D=d),\qquad
 D_{xy}=\operatorname{diag}\{Q_1[x,y],Q_2[x,y]\},
\]
and
\[
 C_y[j,v]=P(X_3=v\mid X_2=y,Z=j,D=d),\qquad v\in\mathcal S.
\]
Here \(C_y\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_2\).  By \(\texttt{ass:consistency}\), \(\texttt{ass:no-anticipation}\), \(\texttt{ass:markov-paths}\), and \(\texttt{ass:common-date-two-transition}\), conditioning first on \(Z\) gives, entry by entry,
\[
 A_{xy}^d[u,v]
 =\sum_{j=1}^2B_x[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y[j,v],
 \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
 A_{xy}^d=B_xD_{xy}C_y.                                      \tag{1}
\]
This factorization uses no time-homogeneity condition.

Let \(\bar C_y=C_y[:,\mathcal A]\).  From (1),
\[
 \bar A_{xy}^d=B_xD_{xy}\bar C_y.                            \tag{2}
\]
Every factor in (2) is \(2\times2\).  By \(\texttt{ass:four-slice-rank}\), each product on the left is nonsingular.  The determinant identity
\[
 \det(\bar A_{xy}^d)=\det(B_x)\det(D_{xy})\det(\bar C_y)
\]
therefore implies that \(B_a,B_b,\bar C_a,\bar C_b\) are nonsingular and that every \(Q_j[x,y]\), for \(x,y\in\mathcal A\), is nonzero.  These entries are probabilities, so they are strictly positive.  In particular, both \(C_a\) and \(C_b\) have row rank two.

Substitution of (2) into the cycle product in \(\texttt{def:observed-slices}\) cancels all adjacent factors and yields
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 K^d
 &=B_aD_{aa}\bar C_a
   (B_bD_{ba}\bar C_a)^{-1}
   B_bD_{bb}\bar C_b
   (B_aD_{ab}\bar C_b)^{-1}\\
 &=B_aD_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}B_a^{-1}\\
 &=B_a\operatorname{diag}(r_1,r_2)B_a^{-1},
 \end{aligned}                                                \tag{3}
\]
where
\[
 r_j=\frac{Q_j[a,a]Q_j[b,b]}{Q_j[b,a]Q_j[a,b]}>0.             \tag{4}
\]
By \(\texttt{ass:simple-cycle-spectrum}\), the two roots are distinct.  Since they are real and positive by (3)--(4), the definitions of \(g^d\) and \(\rho_j^d\) give \(g^d=\rho_1^d-\rho_2^d>0\) and order the two numbers decreasingly.  If \(E_j\) denotes the diagonal matrix with a one in position \(j\), the projector formula in \(\texttt{def:recovery-map}\) and (3) give
\[
 P_j^d=B_aE_jB_a^{-1}.                                       \tag{5}
\]

For \(u\in\mathcal A\), summing over the two types gives
\[
 m_a^d[u]=P(X_0=u,X_1=a\mid D=d)=\sum_{j=1}^2B_a[u,j],
\]
so \(m_a^d=B_a\mathbf1_2\).  Equations (5) and this last identity imply
\[
 P_j^dm_a^d=B_aE_j\mathbf1_2=B_a[:,j].                       \tag{6}
\]
Consequently the matrix called \(B_a^d\) by the recovery map is exactly the latent component predecessor matrix, with both scale and order fixed.

Using (1) with \(x=a\), equations (2) of the recovery map now satisfy
\[
 F_y^d=(B_a^d)^{-1}A_{ay}^d=D_{ay}C_y,
 \qquad
 q_{ay}^d=F_y^d\mathbf1_3=D_{ay}\mathbf1_2.                  \tag{7}
\]
Thus \(q_{ay}^d[j]=Q_j[a,y]>0\), and row-sum normalization gives
\[
 C_y^d=\operatorname{diag}(q_{ay}^d)^{-1}F_y^d=C_y.           \tag{8}
\]
The use of all three terminal columns in (7) is essential: it uses the stochastic equality \(C_y\mathbf1_3=\mathbf1_2\), not a survival probability.

Because \(C_a\) has row rank two,
\[
 C_aC_a^\top\ \text{is positive definite},\qquad
 C_aC_a^\top(C_aC_a^\top)^{-1}=I_2,
\]
and hence \(C_a^\dagger=C_a^\top(C_aC_a^\top)^{-1}\) is a right inverse: \(C_aC_a^\dagger=I_2\).  Equations (1) and (8) therefore give
\[
 W^d=A_{ba}^dC_a^\dagger=B_bD_{ba}.                          \tag{9}
\]
The right side is nonsingular.  Since \(m_b^d=B_b\mathbf1_2\),
\[
 c^d=(W^d)^{-1}m_b^d=D_{ba}^{-1}\mathbf1_2>0,
 \qquad
 W^d\operatorname{diag}(c^d)=B_b.                            \tag{10}
\]
Thus the recovered \(B_b^d\) is exact.  Repeating (7) with \(x=b\) gives
\[
 (B_b^d)^{-1}A_{by}^d\mathbf1_3=D_{by}\mathbf1_2,
\]
which recovers the two active entries of every active row of \(Q_j\).  Row stochasticity recovers the exit entry as
\[
 Q_j[x,e]=1-Q_j[x,a]-Q_j[x,b],
\]
and \(\texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}\) recovers the exit row as \((0,0,1)\).  Equations (8) and absorption likewise recover every row of the factual date-\(3\) kernel, namely \(\widehat R_j^d\).

It remains to verify the component masses.  By \(\texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption}\),
\[
 0=P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=\sum_{j=1}^2P(X_1=e,Z=j\mid D=d).
\]
Each summand is nonnegative, so each is zero.  By \(\texttt{ass:type-overlap}\), conditioning on either type is legitimate.  Moreover, absorption and consistency imply that \(X_0=e\) would force \(X_1=e\); hence there is no omitted predecessor mass.  It follows that
\[
 \pi_j^d=P(Z=j\mid D=d)
 =\sum_{u\in\mathcal A}\{B_a[u,j]+B_b[u,j]\}
 =\widehat\pi_j^d.                                           \tag{11}
\]
Writing
\[
 s_j^d=\bigl(\mathbf1_2^\top B_a[:,j],\mathbf1_2^\top B_b[:,j],0\bigr),
\]
equation (11) shows that \(s_j^d/\pi_j^d\) is the conditional law of \(X_1\) given \((D=d,Z=j)\).  The date-\(2\) Markov recursion then gives
\[
 P(X_2\in\cdot\mid D=d,Z=j)
 =(\pi_j^d)^{-1}s_j^dQ_j=\widehat p_{2,j}^d.                  \tag{12}
\]

Equations (1), (6)--(12), and absorption recover every supported component probability through date \(3\).  Explicitly, for \(u,x,y\in\mathcal A\) and \(v\in\mathcal S\), it is
\[
 B_x[u,j]Q_j[x,y]R_j^d[y,v],                                 \tag{13}
\]
while for \(y=e\) it is
\[
 B_x[u,j]Q_j[x,e]\mathbf1\{v=e\}.                           \tag{14}
\]
No other path has positive probability under the support assumptions.

The matrices \(Q_j\) are common across cohorts by \(\texttt{ass:common-date-two-transition}\), so the two values in (4) are the same in both cohorts.  Their strict separation aligns labels across cohorts even if the mixture weights are equal or differ.  By consistency, controls reveal \(R_j^0=U_j\).  By no anticipation, the treated cohort has the same conditional date-\(2\) law under the two potential paths; by \(\texttt{ass:common-first-post-untreated-transition}\), its untreated date-\(3\) kernel is also \(U_j=R_j^0\).  Therefore conditioning on \((Z,X_2)\) gives the causal contrast
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \tau_j
 &=E\{\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\mid D=1,Z=j\}\\
 &=p_{2,j}^1(R_j^1-R_j^0),\\
 \tau&=\sum_{j=1}^2\pi_j^1\tau_j.                            \tag{15}
 \end{aligned}
\]
Thus (15) equals the final formula defining \(\Phi(p)\), proving \(\Phi(p)=\theta\).

Every step above begins from observable arrays and holds for every \(\widetilde P\in\mathcal F(p)\).  Hence (3), (6)--(12), and (15) take the same values throughout that fiber, which proves the stronger fiberwise assertion.  Finally, no equality between transition matrices at different dates was used.  At the exit cut, absorption makes both terminal rows equal to \((0,0,1)\), so an all-state terminal factor has rank one and strict positivity of all transitions fails.  The proof only requires the four active minors; it therefore applies on precisely this structurally singular absorbing face.

Let \(q_d(p)=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}p_s\).  By \(\texttt{ass:cohort-overlap}\), \(q_d(p)>0\), and every cohort-conditional entry used in \(A_{xy}^d\) and \(m_x^d\) is a linear function of \(p\) divided by \(q_d(p)\).  The proof of \(\texttt{thm:face-recovery}\) shows at every compatible regular \(p\) that all four slice determinants, \(\det(B_a^d)\), \(\det(W^d)\), \(\det(B_b^d)\), every row-sum normalizer used in division, every recovered type mass, and every \(\det\{C_y^d(C_y^d)^\top\}\) are nonzero, while the discriminant \((g^d)^2\) is strictly positive.

Let \(\mathcal U_p\) be the set in the affine hyperplane \(\{z:\mathbf1^\top z=1\}\) on which the same finitely many denominators remain nonzero and both discriminants remain positive.  These are strict conditions on continuous functions, so \(\mathcal U_p\) is a relative open neighborhood of \(p\).  Cohort conditioning and matrix inversion are rational maps there.  The positive square-root function is real analytic on \((0,\infty)\), and
\[
 C^\dagger=C^\top(CC^\top)^{-1}                              \tag{16}
\]
is analytic whenever \(CC^\top\) is nonsingular.  The construction in \(\texttt{def:recovery-map}\) is a finite composition of these rational maps, the positive square root, sums, and products.  Hence \(\Phi\) is real analytic on \(\mathcal U_p\).  Notice that this is an off-model analytic extension: coordinates of \(z\in\mathcal U_p\) need not all be nonnegative.

For completeness, the Jacobian is actionable rather than merely existential.  For a tangent direction \(h\) with \(\mathbf1^\top h=0\), put a dot over every recovered quantity to denote its directional derivative.  First,
\[
 \dot q_d=\sum_{s:D(s)=d}h_s,
 \qquad
 \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\frac{p_s+\varepsilon h_s}{q_d(p+\varepsilon h)}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=0}
 =\frac{h_s}{q_d}-\frac{p_s\dot q_d}{q_d^2}.                 \tag{17}
\]
All slice derivatives follow by the indicated marginal sums.  The remaining recursion is
\[
 \dot M^{-1}=-M^{-1}\dot M M^{-1},\qquad
 \dot g=\frac{2\operatorname{tr}(K)\operatorname{tr}(\dot K)-4\dot{\det K}}{2g},                 \tag{18}
\]
where, for a \(2\times2\) matrix,
\[
 \dot{\det K}=K_{22}\dot K_{11}+K_{11}\dot K_{22}-K_{21}\dot K_{12}-K_{12}\dot K_{21}.         \tag{19}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
 \dot\rho_{1,2}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(\dot K)\mathbin{\pm}\dot g}{2},\quad
 \dot P_1=\frac{\dot K-\dot\rho_2I_2}{g}-\frac{\dot g}{g}P_1,
 \quad \dot P_2=-\dot P_1,                                  \tag{20}
\]
and
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dot B_a[:,j]&=\dot P_jm_a+P_j\dot m_a,\\
 \dot F_y&=-B_a^{-1}\dot B_aF_y+B_a^{-1}\dot A_{ay},\\
 \dot q_{ay}&=\dot F_y\mathbf1_3,\\
 \dot C_y[j,:]&=\{\dot F_y[j,:]-\dot q_{ay}[j]C_y[j,:]\}/q_{ay}[j].
 \end{aligned}                                                \tag{21}
\]
With \(C=C_a\) and \(N=(CC^\top)^{-1}\), differentiation of (16) gives
\[
 \dot C^\dagger=\dot C^\top N-C^\top N(\dot C C^\top+C\dot C^\top)N,                          \tag{22}
\]
followed by
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dot W&=\dot A_{ba}C^\dagger+A_{ba}\dot C^\dagger,\\
 \dot c&=W^{-1}(\dot m_b-\dot Wc),\\
 \dot B_b&=\dot W\operatorname{diag}(c)+W\operatorname{diag}(\dot c).
 \end{aligned}                                                \tag{23}
\]
For \(y\in\mathcal A\), the second-row normalizers satisfy
\[
 \dot q_{by}=-B_b^{-1}\dot B_bq_{by}+B_b^{-1}\dot A_{by}\mathbf1_3.
\]
Thus the active entries of \(\dot{\widehat Q}_j^d\) are \(\dot q_{ay}[j]\) and \(\dot q_{by}[j]\); its exit entry is minus their sum, and its absorbing-row derivative is zero.  The active rows of \(\dot{\widehat R}_j^d\) are the corresponding rows of \(\dot C_y^d\), and its absorbing-row derivative is zero.  If
\[
 s_j^d=(\mathbf1_2^\top B_a^d[:,j],\mathbf1_2^\top B_b^d[:,j],0),
\]
then
\[
 \dot\pi_j^d=\mathbf1_2^\top\{\dot B_a^d[:,j]+\dot B_b^d[:,j]\},\quad
 \dot p_{1,j}^d=\frac{\dot s_j^d\pi_j^d-s_j^d\dot\pi_j^d}{(\pi_j^d)^2},\quad
 \dot p_{2,j}^d=\dot p_{1,j}^d\widehat Q_j^d+p_{1,j}^d\dot{\widehat Q}_j^d.                    \tag{24}
\]
Finally,
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \dot\tau_j&=\dot p_{2,j}^1(\widehat R_j^1-\widehat R_j^0)
 +p_{2,j}^1(\dot{\widehat R}_j^1-\dot{\widehat R}_j^0),\\
 \dot\tau&=\sum_{j=1}^2\{\dot\pi_j^1\tau_j+\pi_j^1\dot\tau_j\}.
 \end{aligned}                                                \tag{25}
\]
Equations (17)--(25) determine \(J_\Phi(p)h\), including the derivative of the recovered type weights.

We next prove the canonical-gradient assertion.  Let \(\mathcal S_0\) denote the finite support stratum containing \(p\), and suppose \(p_s>0\) for every \(s\in\mathcal S_0\), which is exactly relative interiority on that stratum.  Every saturated score is a function \(h:\mathcal S_0\to\mathbb R\) satisfying
\[
 E_P h(O)=\sum_{s\in\mathcal S_0}p_sh(s)=0.                  \tag{26}
\]
Conversely, for any bounded such \(h\), \(p_{\varepsilon,s}=p_s\{1+\varepsilon h(s)\}\) is a probability law for all sufficiently small \(|\varepsilon|\), and it has score \(h\).  Thus the saturated tangent space is all of \(L_2^0(P)\).  Differentiability of \(\Phi\), (26), and the definition of \(G_p\) yield
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\Phi(p_\varepsilon)\right|_{\varepsilon=0}
 &=J_\Phi(p)\sum_s p_se_sh(s)\\
 &=E_P\!\left[J_\Phi(p)(e_O-p)h(O)\right]
 =E_P\{G_p(O)h(O)\},                                         \tag{27}
 \end{aligned}
\]
because \(E_Ph=0\).  Also \(E_PG_p(O)=J_\Phi(p)(p-p)=0\).  If \(H\) is any other centered influence function for the same functional, (27) implies \(E_P\{(H-G_p)h\}=0\) for every \(h\in L_2^0(P)\).  Taking each coordinate of \(H-G_p\) itself as \(h\) proves \(H=G_p\) almost surely.  Hence \(G_p\) is the canonical gradient, and its covariance
\[
 E_P\{G_p(O)G_p(O)^\top\}
 =J_\Phi(p)\{\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^\top\}J_\Phi(p)^\top
 =\Sigma(p)                                                     \tag{28}
\]
is the saturated information bound.  This proves the bound rather than identifying it by definition: for any centered influence function \(H\), the score equations force \(H=G_p\), so the infimum of influence-function covariance matrices in the positive-semidefinite order is exactly (28).

For the empirical-cell plug-in, the multinomial identity gives
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat p-p)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(e_{O_i}-p),
 \qquad \widehat p-p=O_P(n^{-1/2}).                           \tag{29}
\]
Taylor expansion of the analytic map at a fixed interior \(p\) and (29) give
\[
 \sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)\}
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nJ_\Phi(p)(e_{O_i}-p)+o_P(1)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i)+o_P(1).                       \tag{30}
\]
Its influence function is therefore the canonical gradient and its asymptotic covariance is (28), so it attains the saturated finite-multinomial information bound.

Let \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) be the set of cell vectors induced by \(\mathcal P_\kappa\).  By \(\texttt{def:buffered-class}\), it is a compact subset of the finite-parameter compatible image.  By \(\texttt{def:margin-vector}\), every inverse, division, eigengap, label, and mass normalization used by \(\Phi\) is among the coordinates of \(\mathfrak m(p)\).  The population inequalities in \(\texttt{ass:margin-buffer}\) put these coordinates at least \(2\kappa\), while \(\texttt{ass:variance-buffer}\) gives \(\Sigma_{\ell\ell}(p)\geq2\kappa\) for \(\ell\in\mathcal L\).

The analyticity proved in \(\texttt{thm:analytic-gradient}\), compactness, and the finite margin list imply that there is a fixed \(r>0\) such that the relative closed \(r\)-neighborhood of \(\mathcal K_\kappa\) lies in the analytic domain and every empirical guard margin there exceeds \(\kappa\).  On that neighborhood there are finite constants
\[
 L_1=\sup_q\|J_\Phi(q)\|<\infty,
 \qquad L_2=\sup_q\|D^2\Phi(q)\|<\infty.                    \tag{31}
\]
The legality part of the guard holds almost surely because every \(P\in\mathcal P_\kappa\) assigns zero probability to forbidden cells.  Direct multinomial variance calculation gives
\[
 E_P\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2
 =\frac{1-\|p\|_2^2}{n}\leq\frac1n.
\]
Since \(\mathbf1\{\|\widehat p-p\|_2>r\}\leq\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2/r^2\), it follows without a cell-probability lower bound that
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}P\{\|\widehat p-p\|_2>r\}
 \leq\frac1{nr^2}.                                            \tag{32}
\]
On the complementary event all sequential calculations are legal and all guard margins exceed \(\kappa\).  Equation (32) proves
\[
 \inf_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}P(\mathcal E_\kappa)\longrightarrow1.                              \tag{33}
\]

On this event Taylor's formula and (31) imply
\[
 \left\|\sqrt n\{\Phi(\widehat p)-\Phi(p)-J_\Phi(p)(\widehat p-p)\}\right\|
 \leq\frac{L_2}{2}\sqrt n\|\widehat p-p\|_2^2.             \tag{34}
\]
Consequently, using the same second-moment calculation, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) the probability that the norm in (34) exceeds \(\varepsilon\) is at most
\[
 \frac1{nr^2}+\frac{L_2}{2\varepsilon\sqrt n},               \tag{35}
\]
uniformly over the class.  By \(\texttt{thm:face-recovery}\), \(\Phi(p)=\theta\) on this class.  Since
\[
 J_\Phi(p)\sqrt n(\widehat p-p)
 =n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i),
\]
(34)--(35) prove the asserted uniform asymptotic linear representation.  On \(\mathcal E_\kappa^c\), one may assign any fixed value to the otherwise unreported estimator; (33) makes this extension asymptotically irrelevant.

The empirical covariance has the exact finite-cell form
\[
 \widehat\Sigma
 =J_\Phi(\widehat p)\{\operatorname{diag}(\widehat p)-\widehat p\widehat p^\top\}J_\Phi(\widehat p)^\top.               \tag{37}
\]
This follows by expanding \(n^{-1}\sum_i(e_{O_i}-\widehat p)(e_{O_i}-\widehat p)^\top\).  The map on the right of (37) is uniformly continuous on the compact neighborhood from (31).  Equations (32) and (37) therefore prove
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}
 P\{\|\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(p)\|>\varepsilon\}\longrightarrow0.                               \tag{38}
\]
In particular, every reported empirical diagonal exceeds \(\kappa\) with probability tending to one uniformly, and studentization never requires inversion of the full covariance matrix.

It remains to prove exact simultaneous coverage, including singular correlation limits.  We use a sequential compactness argument.  Consider an arbitrary sequence \(P_n\in\mathcal P_\kappa\).  Compactness permits passage to a subsequence, still indexed by \(n\), for which \(p_n\to p_\star\).  Continuity gives
\[
 \Sigma(p_n)\to\Sigma(p_\star),\qquad
 \sigma_{n,\ell}^2:=\Sigma_{\ell\ell}(p_n)\geq2\kappa.      \tag{39}
\]
Let \(Y_{n,i}\) be the vector over \(\ell\in\mathcal L\) with entries \(G_{p_n,\ell}(O_i)/\sigma_{n,\ell}\), and let \(\Gamma_n=E_{P_n}(Y_{n,i}Y_{n,i}^\top)\).  The matrices \(\Gamma_n\) have unit diagonal.  Equations (31) and (39) make \(Y_{n,i}\) uniformly bounded, and after another subsequence \(\Gamma_n\to\Gamma_\star\), where \(\Gamma_\star\) may be singular.

For every fixed vector \(u\), centering and a third-order Taylor expansion of the exponential give, uniformly on this subsequence,
\[
 E_{P_n}\exp\{i u^\top Y_{n,1}/\sqrt n\}
 =1-\frac{u^\top\Gamma_nu}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2}).                  \tag{40}
\]
Independence in \(\texttt{ass:iid-panels}\) and (40) imply
\[
 E_{P_n}\exp\left\{iu^\top n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nY_{n,i}\right\}
 =\left(1-\frac{u^\top\Gamma_nu}{2n}+O(n^{-3/2})\right)^n
 \longrightarrow\exp(-u^\top\Gamma_\star u/2).              \tag{41}
\]
Thus the studentized linear term converges to \(Z_\star\sim N(0,\Gamma_\star)\); the characteristic-function calculation remains valid when \(\Gamma_\star\) is singular.

Conditionally on the sample, the multiplier numerator is exactly Gaussian because the \(\xi_i\) are independent standard Gaussian variables.  After coordinatewise studentization its covariance is the empirical correlation matrix
\[
 \widehat\Gamma_{ell k}
 =\widehat\Sigma_{ell k}/
 \sqrt{\widehat\Sigma_{ell\ell}\widehat\Sigma_{kk}}.        \tag{42}
\]
Equations (38)--(39) yield \(\widehat\Gamma\to\Gamma_\star\) in \(P_n\)-probability.  The proved result \(\texttt{lem:gaussian-max-quantile-continuity}\), applied with \(u=1-\alpha\), shows that
\[
 \widehat c_{1-\alpha}\longrightarrow c_\star               \tag{43}
\]
in probability, where \(c_\star\) is the unique \(1-\alpha\) quantile of \(\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}|Z_{\star,\ell}|\).  The same proved result shows that this maximum has no atom at \(c_\star\) and
\[
 P\{\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}|Z_{\star,\ell}|\leq c_\star\}=1-\alpha.                           \tag{44}
\]

The asymptotic linear representation, (38)--(41), and the positive diagonal bound in (39) show that the coverage event is asymptotically equivalent to
\[
 \left\{\max_{\ell\in\mathcal L}
 \frac{|n^{-1/2}\sum_iG_{p_n,\ell}(O_i)|}{\sigma_{n,\ell}}
 \leq \widehat c_{1-\alpha}\right\}.
\]
Equations (43)--(44) therefore give coverage tending to \(1-\alpha\) along the selected subsequence.  Because the original sequence was arbitrary, a contradiction-subsequence argument yields
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\kappa}
 \left|P\{\theta_\ell\in I_{\ell,n}\text{ for all }\ell\in\mathcal L\}-(1-\alpha)\right|
 \longrightarrow0.                                           \tag{45}
\]
The displayed infimum in the theorem follows from (45).  At no point was a positive smallest eigenvalue of \(\Sigma(p)\) or of its correlation matrix assumed.

theorem.statement:
At every law \(P\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\) at which the constrained tangent space \(\mathcal T_P\) is defined on its actual finite support, the constrained efficient influence function is the coordinatewise orthogonal projection \(\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P}=\Pi_{\mathcal T_P}G_p\), and the constrained efficiency bound is \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)=E_P\{\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P}(O)\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P}(O)^\top\}\).  For every \(a\in\mathbb R^9\),
\[
 a^\top\{\Sigma(p)-V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\}a
 =\|(I-\Pi_{\mathcal T_P})a^\top G_p\|_{L_2(P)}^2.
\]
Thus the constrained bound is strictly smaller than the saturated bound in direction \(a\) exactly when \(a^\top G_p\notin\mathcal T_P\).  On any smooth local stratum with constant tangent rank, the projection is computable from a finite score matrix by weighted least squares, which is the finite implementation of \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{eff}}\), and a regular local likelihood or one-step estimator attains this bound pointwise.  The frozen definition of \(\mathcal P_\kappa\) does not buffer support changes or the rank of that score matrix, so these conclusions do not by themselves establish uniform constrained efficiency on all of \(\mathcal P_\kappa\).
theorem.proof_tex:
Fix \(P\) and let \(\langle f,h\rangle_P=E_P\{f(O)h(O)\}\).  By \(\texttt{thm:face-recovery}\), the causal target agrees with \(\Phi(p)\) on every constrained parametric submodel through \(P\).  By \(\texttt{thm:analytic-gradient}\), for every score \(h\in\mathcal T_P\),
\[
 \dot\theta_P[h]=E_P\{G_p(O)h(O)\}.                           \tag{46}
\]
The space \(\mathcal T_P\) is closed by definition, so its orthogonal projection exists.  Put \(\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}=\Pi_{\mathcal T_P}G_{p,\ell}\).  Then \(\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}\in\mathcal T_P\) and, because \(G_{p,\ell}-\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}\) is orthogonal to \(\mathcal T_P\),
\[
 \dot\theta_{P,\ell}[h]
 =\langle G_{p,\ell},h\rangle_P
 =\langle\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell},h\rangle_P
 \quad\text{for every }h\in\mathcal T_P.                    \tag{47}
\]
If another element of \(\mathcal T_P\) represents the same derivative, its difference from \(\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}\) is both in \(\mathcal T_P\) and orthogonal to \(\mathcal T_P\), hence is zero.  This proves the efficient-influence-function characterization and the covariance formula for \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\).

Write \(R_\ell=(I-\Pi_{\mathcal T_P})G_{p,\ell}\).  Orthogonality gives
\[
 \Sigma_{\ell k}(p)
 =\langle\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell},\psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,k}\rangle_P
  +\langle R_\ell,R_k\rangle_P.                              \tag{48}
\]
Therefore \(\Sigma(p)-V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\) is the Gram matrix of the residuals.  For \(a\in\mathbb R^9\), (48) gives
\[
 a^\top\{\Sigma(p)-V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\}a
 =\left\|\sum_{\ell=1}^9a_\ell R_\ell\right\|_{L_2(P)}^2
 =\|(I-\Pi_{\mathcal T_P})a^\top G_p\|_{L_2(P)}^2,           \tag{49}
\]
which proves both positive-semidefinite dominance and the stated necessary-and-sufficient strictness criterion.

We now expose a computable version of the projection required by \(\mathfrak H_{\mathrm{eff}}\).  Enumerate the actual support as \(s=1,\ldots,m_P\), let \(W_P=\operatorname{diag}(p_1,ldots,p_{m_P})\), and choose any finite score-generator matrix \(S_P\) whose columns span \(\mathcal T_P\).  Such a matrix is obtained by differentiating the finite latent-mixture, absorbing-support, common-kernel, and date-\(4\) polynomial parameterization and deleting linearly redundant columns.  For coordinate \(\ell\), solve the explicit weighted least-squares problem
\[
 \min_{\beta\in\mathbb R^{k_P}}
 \sum_{s=1}^{m_P}p_s\{G_{p,\ell}(s)-S_P[s,:]\beta\}^2.       \tag{50}
\]
Its normal equations and fitted value are
\[
 S_P^\top W_PS_P\beta=S_P^\top W_PG_{p,\ell},\qquad
 \psi_{\mathrm{eff},P,\ell}
 =S_P(S_P^\top W_PS_P)^\dagger S_P^\top W_PG_{p,\ell}.      \tag{51}
\]
The Moore--Penrose inverse makes (51) invariant to redundant generators; the fitted value, unlike \(\beta\), is unique.  Equations (50)--(51) are the promised finite computation, and the fifth-date and common-kernel information enter through the columns of \(S_P\).

On a smooth local stratum, select independent score columns and a local parameter \(\eta\).  With \(I_P=S_P^\top W_PS_P\), the likelihood score equation has the first-order expansion
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat\eta-\eta)
 =I_P^{-1}n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n S_P[O_i,:]^\top+o_P(1).        \tag{52}
\]
The derivative of coordinate \(\theta_\ell\) with respect to \(\eta\) is, by (46),
\[
 \dot\theta_{\ell,\eta}=G_{p,\ell}^\top W_PS_P.              \tag{53}
\]
Combining (52)--(53) gives precisely the fitted influence function in (51).  Hence a regular local likelihood estimator, or the algebraically equivalent one-step estimator, attains \(V_{\mathrm{eff}}(P)\) pointwise whenever the smooth constant-rank expansion (52) is valid.

Finally, \(\texttt{def:buffered-class}\) bounds the recovery margins and the reported saturated variances, but it contains no lower bound on the positive singular values of \(S_P^\top W_PS_P\), no constant-rank condition, and no distance from additional date-\(4\) support boundaries.  For example, an allowed date-\(4\) transition probability may approach zero while all date-\(0\)-through-date-\(3\) slices, \(\Phi(p)\), and their recovery margins remain fixed.  Thus the uniform Taylor expansion needed for (52) is not supplied by the frozen assumptions.  The pointwise characterization (46)--(53) and exact strictness criterion (49) are proved, whereas uniform attainment on the whole buffered class requires an additional tangent-rank and support-margin analysis and is not asserted here.

added_lemmas.statement: Fix a positive integer \(q\).  Let \(\Gamma_n\) and \(\Gamma\) be positive-semidefinite \(q\times q\) matrices with unit diagonal and \(\Gamma_n\to\Gamma\).  If \(Z_n\sim N(0,\Gamma_n)\) and \(Z\sim N(0,\Gamma)\), allowing every matrix to be singular, then the distribution function of \(\max_{1\leq k\leq q}|Z_k|\) is continuous and strictly increasing on \([0,\infty)\), and the \(u\)-quantiles of \(\max_k|Z_{n,k}|\) converge to its \(u\)-quantile for every \(u\in(0,1)\).
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
Let \(L=\operatorname{range}(\Gamma^{1/2})\).  Since every diagonal entry of \(\Gamma\) is one, \(L\neq\{0\}\), and the law of \(Z\) has a strictly positive Gaussian density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(L\).  The restriction \(x\mapsto\|x\|_\infty\) to \(L\) is a norm.  For any \(0\leq s<t\), choose nonzero \(x\in L\) and rescale it so that \(s<\|x\|_\infty<t\).  The set
\[
 \{y\in L:s<\|y\|_\infty<t\}
\]
then contains a nonempty relatively open subset of \(L\), and therefore has strictly positive Gaussian probability.  Thus the distribution function is strictly increasing.

For \(t\geq0\),
\[
 \{\|Z\|_\infty=t\}\subseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^q\{|Z_k|=t\}.
\]
Each marginal \(Z_k\) is \(N(0,1)\), even when the joint covariance is singular, so every event in the finite union has probability zero.  The distribution function is consequently continuous.  Its value at zero is zero and it tends to one at infinity, so its \(u\)-quantile \(c_u(\Gamma)\) is unique for every \(u\in(0,1)\).

For every \(v\in\mathbb R^q\), the characteristic functions satisfy
\[
 E\exp(i v^\top Z_n)=\exp(-v^\top\Gamma_nv/2)\longrightarrow
 \exp(-v^\top\Gamma v/2)=E\exp(i v^\top Z),
\]
so \(Z_n\) converges in distribution to \(Z\).  Since the maximum norm is continuous, the corresponding maxima converge in distribution.  If \(F_n,F\) are their distribution functions and \(c=c_u(\Gamma)\), strict increase and continuity give, for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
 F(c-\varepsilon)<u<F(c+\varepsilon).
\]
Convergence at these two continuity points gives the same strict inequalities for \(F_n\) for all large \(n\), whence
\[
 c-\varepsilon<c_u(\Gamma_n)<c+\varepsilon.
\]
Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) proves quantile convergence without any lower bound on the smallest eigenvalue.

proposed.statement: The map \(\Phi\) extends real analytically to an open neighborhood of every regular \(p\) satisfying the identification assumptions. In the saturated finite-multinomial model on the declared support stratum, \(G_p(s)=J_{\Phi}(p)(e_s-p)\) is the canonical gradient of \(\Phi(p)\), \(\Sigma(p)\) is its information bound, and the empirical-cell plug-in attains this bound at every relative-interior law on that stratum.
proposed.justification: Analyticity makes the influence function explicit and turns a constructive identification formula into a regular finite-multinomial estimator.
proposed.gap: Bonhomme, Jochmans, and Robin differentiate simultaneous-diagonalization estimators for nonexchangeable latent models, while Ahn and Kasahara use interior likelihood asymptotics; neither gives the canonical gradient of this row-sum and pseudoinverse map on an absorbing support stratum.
proposed.consumer: Implementers obtain a closed-form delta-method variance that includes estimated type masses and avoids repeated nonconvex likelihood optimization.

proposed_core_edits.reason: The analyticity proof uses the recovery theorem to establish that every normalization and pseudoinverse denominator is nonzero at compatible laws; this dependency must be explicit in the proof spine.

proposed.statement: Uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal P_{\kappa}\), \(P(\mathcal E_{\kappa})\to1\), \(\sqrt n\{\widehat\theta-\theta\}=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nG_p(O_i)+o_P(1)\), and \(\widehat\Sigma-\Sigma(p)=o_P(1)\). Moreover, allowing \(\Sigma(p)\) to be singular while retaining its buffered reported diagonal, \(\inf_{P\in\mathcal P_{\kappa}}P(\theta_\ell\in I_{\ell,n}\text{ for every }\ell\in\mathcal L)\to1-\alpha\).
proposed.justification: The coverage theorem integrates data-dependent numerical guards with a singular-correlation Gaussian maximum, the unresolved proof boundary left by pointwise interior theory.
proposed.gap: Chernozhukov, Chetverikov, and Kato allow arbitrary Gaussian correlation under positive marginal variances, but do not study a guarded rational spectral map; Ahn and Kasahara's weighted-bootstrap intervals do not establish uniform acceptance and coverage on an absorbing face.
proposed.consumer: Users can report joint bands for all type-specific and aggregate state effects even when adding-up identities make the nine-dimensional covariance singular.

proposed_core_edits.reason: Uniform causal centering uses face recovery, the guard proof uses the complete margin-vector definition, and singular-correlation coverage uses the proved Gaussian quantile-continuity lemma; all three dependencies must be explicit.

proofs.proof_tex:
We first verify that the construction in \texttt{def:exact-witness} defines a law with every property required by \texttt{def:face-model}.  A convenient explicit coupling of the two potential paths is the following.  Put \(R_{j,0}=Q_j\) and \(R_{j,1}=V_j\).  For \(d\in\{0,1\}\), \(j\in\{1,2\}\), \(s_0\in\mathcal A\), and all remaining states in \(\mathcal S\), define the joint mass of
\[
 (D,Z,S_0,S_1,S_2,X_3(0),X_4(0),X_3(1),X_4(1))
 =(d,j,s_0,s_1,s_2,u_0,w_0,u_1,w_1)
\]
to be
\[
 \frac18 H_j[s_0,s_1]Q_j[s_1,s_2]
 Q_j[s_2,u_0]Q_j[u_0,w_0]
 V_j[s_2,u_1]V_j[u_1,w_1],                                      \tag{1}
\]
and give mass zero when \(s_0\notin\mathcal A\).  Every displayed matrix has nonnegative entries and satisfies
\[
 H_j\mathbf 1_3=Q_j\mathbf 1_3=V_j\mathbf 1_3=\mathbf 1_3,
 \qquad
 H_j[e,{:}]=Q_j[e,{:}]=V_j[e,{:}]=(0,0,1).                       \tag{2}
\]
Consequently, summing (1) successively over \(w_0,u_0,w_1,u_1,s_2,s_1,s_0,j,d\) gives one, so (1) is a probability law.  Set \(X_t(r)=S_t\) for \(t\leq2\) and \(r\in\{0,1\}\), and set the observed state to \(X_t=X_t(D)\).  This proves consistency and no anticipation.  Marginalizing the continuation belonging to the other treatment path in (1) leaves a first-order Markov factorization conditional on \((D,Z)\): its transitions are \(H_j,Q_j,Q_j,Q_j\) for \(r=0\) and \(H_j,Q_j,V_j,V_j\) for \(r=1\).  Thus \texttt{ass:markov-paths} holds.  Equation (2), together with inspection of the active rows in \texttt{def:exact-witness}, proves support on \(\mathcal G\) and \texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}.  Moreover,
\[
 P(D=d)=\frac12,\qquad P(Z=j\mid D=d)=\frac12,                 \tag{3}
\]
so cohort and type overlap hold and both type support points occur.  Taking \(H_j^d=H_j\), \(U_j=Q_j\), and \(L_j=Q_j\) verifies all three declared common untreated-transition restrictions.  Finally, \(S_0\in\mathcal A\) almost surely and \(H_j[x,e]=0\) for \(x\in\mathcal A\), whence
\[
 P(X_1=e\mid D=d)=0                                             \tag{4}
\]
for both cohorts.  This verifies \texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption}.

It remains to check the two rank conditions and the numerical conclusions.  For \(x\in\mathcal A\), introduce the component predecessor matrix
\[
 B_x[u,j]=P(X_0=u,X_1=x,Z=j\mid D=d)
          =\frac14H_j[u,x].                                     \tag{5}
\]
It does not depend on \(d\), and direct substitution gives
\[
 B_a=\begin{pmatrix}3/16&1/12\\1/16&1/6\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 B_b=\begin{pmatrix}1/16&1/6\\3/16&1/12\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 \det(B_a)=\frac5{192},\quad \det(B_b)=-\frac5{192}.           \tag{6}
\]
Let \(D_{xy}=\operatorname{diag}(Q_1[x,y],Q_2[x,y])\), and let row \(j\) of \(C_y^0\) be row \(y\) of \(Q_j\), while row \(j\) of \(C_y^1\) is row \(y\) of \(V_j\).  Conditional first-order Markov factorization and summation over \(Z\) yield, entry by entry,
\[
 A_{xy}^d[u,v]
 =\sum_{j=1}^2B_x[u,j]Q_j[x,y]C_y^d[j,v],
 \qquad A_{xy}^d=B_xD_{xy}C_y^d.                                \tag{7}
\]
For the active terminal minors, direct calculation gives
\[
 \det(\bar C_a^0)=\frac9{50},\quad
 \det(\bar C_b^0)=-\frac3{100},\quad
 \det(\bar C_a^1)=\frac{31}{100},\quad
 \det(\bar C_b^1)=-\frac1{20}.                                 \tag{8}
\]
Using \(\det(\bar A_{xy}^d)=\det(B_x)Q_1[x,y]Q_2[x,y]\det(\bar C_y^d)\), equations (6)--(8) give, in the order \((aa,ab,ba,bb)\),
\[
 \bigl(\det\bar A_{aa}^0,\det\bar A_{ab}^0,
       \det\bar A_{ba}^0,\det\bar A_{bb}^0\bigr)
 =\left(\frac9{16000},-\frac3{32000},-\frac9{32000},\frac3{12800}\right), \tag{9}
\]
and
\[
 \bigl(\det\bar A_{aa}^1,\det\bar A_{ab}^1,
       \det\bar A_{ba}^1,\det\bar A_{bb}^1\bigr)
 =\left(\frac{31}{32000},-\frac1{6400},-\frac{31}{64000},\frac1{2560}\right). \tag{10}
\]
Every number in (9)--(10) is nonzero.  Hence every one of the eight active slices is nonsingular; since there are finitely many of them, the minimum of their positive smallest singular values is positive.  This is exactly \texttt{ass:four-slice-rank}.

Restricting (7) to active terminal columns and multiplying the four factors in the order specified by \texttt{def:observed-slices} cancels \(\bar C_a^d,B_b,\bar C_b^d\) and gives
\[
 K^d
 =B_aD_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}B_a^{-1}.              \tag{11}
\]
All divisions in (11) are legitimate because the relevant active entries of \(Q_1,Q_2\) are strictly positive.  The middle diagonal matrix is
\[
 D_{aa}D_{ba}^{-1}D_{bb}D_{ab}^{-1}
 =\operatorname{diag}\!\left(
 \frac{(3/5)(1/2)}{(1/5)(3/10)},
 \frac{(1/5)(3/5)}{(3/10)(2/5)}\right)
 =\operatorname{diag}(5,1).                                    \tag{12}
\]
Writing \(B_a=48^{-1}\begin{psmallmatrix}9&4\\3&8\end{psmallmatrix}\), equations (11)--(12) therefore imply, for both \(d=0\) and \(d=1\),
\[
 K^d
 =\frac1{60}
 \begin{pmatrix}45&4\\15&8\end{pmatrix}
 \begin{pmatrix}8&-4\\-3&9\end{pmatrix}
 =\begin{pmatrix}29/5&-12/5\\8/5&1/5\end{pmatrix}.             \tag{13}
\]
Its trace and determinant are \(6\) and \(5\), respectively, so
\[
 \det(\lambda I_2-K^d)=\lambda^2-6\lambda+5=(\lambda-5)(\lambda-1),
 \qquad g^d=\sqrt{6^2-4\cdot5}=4>0.                            \tag{14}
\]
Thus the ordered spectrum is \((5,1)\), and \texttt{ass:simple-cycle-spectrum} holds.  Equations (2)--(4), (9)--(10), and (14), together with the preceding structural checks, verify every member property in \texttt{def:face-model}; hence \(\omega^\star\in\mathcal M_{\mathrm{face}}\).

We next compute the causal effects rather than defining them from the observed recovery formula.  The uniform initial law is invariant under each \(H_j\), and therefore the type-specific date-two laws in the treated cohort are
\[
 p_{2,1}^1=(1/2,1/2,0)H_1Q_1=(2/5,2/5,1/5),
 \qquad
 p_{2,2}^1=(1/2,1/2,0)H_2Q_2=(1/4,1/2,1/4).                    \tag{15}
\]
By no anticipation in the coupling (1), both potential paths have the same \(X_2\); conditioning on \((X_2,Z,D=1)\) and using the transition factors in (1) thus yields the causal identity
\[
 \tau_j=p_{2,j}^1(V_j-Q_j).                                    \tag{16}
\]
The two multiplications in (16) are
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \tau_1
 &= (2/5,2/5,1/5)
 \begin{pmatrix}1/10&-1/10&0\\0&1/10&-1/10\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
   =(1/25,0,-1/25),\\
 \tau_2
 &= (1/4,1/2,1/4)
 \begin{pmatrix}0&1/10&-1/10\\-1/20&-1/10&3/20\\0&0&0\end{pmatrix}
   =(-1/40,-1/40,1/20).
 \end{aligned}                                                  \tag{17}
\]
This derives the potential-outcome contrasts in the proposition directly from the constructed law.  By (3) and the definition of the aggregate ATT,
\[
 \tau=\frac12\tau_1+\frac12\tau_2
      =(3/400,-1/80,1/200).                                    \tag{18}
\]

Finally consider \texttt{def:outside-face-pair}.  Let the added component have \(X_t(0)=X_t(1)=e\) for every \(t\).  Conditional on either cohort, both \(P^A\) and \(P^B\) put mass \(4/5\) on the law \(\omega^\star\) and mass \(1/5\) on this all-exit path; they differ only in whether the latent label of the added component is \(1\) or \(2\).  Thus for every state path \(x_{0:4}\),
\[
 P^A(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
 =P^B(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
 =\frac45P_{\omega^\star}(X_{0:4}=x_{0:4}\mid D=d)
  +\frac15\mathbf 1\{x_{0:4}=(e,e,e,e,e)\}.                   \tag{19}
\]
The cohort law is also the same, so (19) proves equality of the complete observed five-date laws.  The two enlarged laws retain all assumptions in \texttt{def:face-model} except (4).  In particular, the conditional Markov property is not lost by mixing: at any active current state the all-exit component has posterior probability zero, so the next-state row is the original active row; at current state \(e\), both mixture components move to \(e\) with probability one by \texttt{ass:absorbing-exit}.  Hence the transition depends only on the current state, \((D,Z)\), and the relevant date, and every common untreated kernel remains \(Q_j\) on active rows with absorbing row \((0,0,1)\).  On the other hand,
\[
 P^A(X_1=e\mid D=d)=P^B(X_1=e\mid D=d)=\frac15,                \tag{20}
\]
so these laws lie outside precisely the declared no-date-one-absorption face.

Because the all-exit path contributes to none of the slices indexed by \(x,y\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 A_{xy}^{A,d}=A_{xy}^{B,d}=\frac45A_{xy}^{\omega^\star,d},
 \qquad
 \bar A_{xy}^{A,d}=\bar A_{xy}^{B,d}=\frac45\bar A_{xy}^{\omega^\star,d}. \tag{21}
\]
Thus all active slices remain nonsingular.  The four scalar factors in the cycle product cancel as
\[
 \left(\frac45\right)
 \left(\frac45\right)^{-1}
 \left(\frac45\right)
 \left(\frac45\right)^{-1}=1,                                 \tag{22}
\]
so both laws retain the matrix (13) and its ordered type signatures \(5>1\).  The active part has conditional mass \((4/5)(1/2)=2/5\) for each type.  Allocation of the added \(1/5\) therefore gives
\[
 (\pi_1^{A,d},\pi_2^{A,d})=(3/5,2/5),
 \qquad
 (\pi_1^{B,d},\pi_2^{B,d})=(2/5,3/5).                          \tag{23}
\]
The all-exit component has state-effect vector \(\mathbf e_e-\mathbf e_e=0\).  Hence, for \(C\in\{A,B\}\), the conditional-effect numerators obey
\[
 \pi_j^{C,1}\tau_j^C
 =E_C\!\left[\mathbf 1\{Z=j\}
   \{\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(1))-\operatorname{onehot}(X_3(0))\}
   \mid D=1\right]
 =\frac25\tau_j^{\omega^\star}.                               \tag{24}
\]
Dividing (24) by the strictly positive masses in (23), and then taking the exit coordinate of (17), gives
\[
 (\tau_{1,e}^A,\tau_{2,e}^A)=(-2/75,1/20),
 \qquad
 (\tau_{1,e}^B,\tau_{2,e}^B)=(-1/25,1/30).                     \tag{25}
\]
Their common aggregate exit effect is nevertheless
\[
 \tau_e^C=\sum_{j=1}^2\pi_j^{C,1}\tau_{j,e}^C
 =\frac25\left(-\frac1{25}+\frac1{20}\right)=\frac1{250},
 \qquad C\in\{A,B\}.                                         \tag{26}
\]
Equations (19), (23), and (25) exhibit two laws in the model obtained by deleting \texttt{ass:no-date-one-absorption} that have the same observed law but different type masses and different conditional type effects.  Therefore no functional of that observed law can equal either of those conditional latent-type targets throughout the enlarged compatible fiber.  Equation (26) records, without overclaiming, that this particular pair does not separate the aggregate exit ATT.
